studies.label: Laboratory experiment: creativity acquisition and transfer after AI instruction, human instruction, or quiet rest

counts_source.locator: PDF p. 1, Abstract (total randomized); PDF p. 3, Section 2.1 Participants (randomized arm counts); two verbatim excerpts
counts_source.quote:
95 participants were randomized into AI instruction, human instruction, or control conditions.
AI (n = 31, 27 females), human (n = 34, 21 females), and control (n = 30, 28 females).

arms.name: AI instruction
arms.description: Real-time text dialogue with ChatGPT-4.0 as a creativity instructor, with standardized example prompts and backup strategy materials; participants could request more original ideas. PDF p. 4, Section 2.3.

arms.name: Human instruction
arms.description: Individual face-to-face heuristic instruction from trained postgraduate education students following standardized creativity-teaching scripts. PDF p. 4, Section 2.3.

arms.name: Control
arms.description: Quiet rest with eyes closed for the same duration, without instruction or interaction. PDF p. 4, Section 2.3.

studies.country: China (inferred from Shanghai Normal University affiliations and ethics approval; participant country is not explicitly stated)
studies.task: Generate alternative uses for books before and after instruction and for umbrellas and can at post-test, scored separately as creativity acquisition and transfer.

ai_tool.name: ChatGPT-4.0
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 4, Section 2.3: "participants interacted directly with ChatGPT-4.0 in real time"; model release year and dated version are not stated.

estimates.question: after_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Two trained independent raters rated each idea on a five-point scale from not at all original to very original after pooling responses and removing duplicates; rater scores were averaged to produce participant scores. The aggregation of idea ratings within a participant is not specified. PDF p. 3, Section 2.2.

sources.locator: PDF p. 5, Section 3.1, Learning outcome; PDF p. 6, Fig. 2 caption (standard-deviation convention); two verbatim excerpts
sources.quote:
Post hoc comparisons revealed that, within the AI instruction group, the scores of post-test fluency (11.29 ± 2.91), originality (34.91 ± 10.80) and flexibility (7.29 ± 2.97)
Error bars indicate standard deviations.

sources.locator: PDF p. 3, Section 2.2, Assessment of creativity
sources.quote: Their ratings were then averaged to yield each participant's fluency, originality, and flexibility scores.

sources.locator: PDF p. 5, Section 3.1, Learning outcome
sources.quote: Moreover, the post-test originality and flexibility scores also significantly higher than the posttest scores of human instructor group and control group, ps ≤0.04.

estimates.notes: Post-test arm levels, not pre-post change scores. The comparison-arm mean and SD appear only as bars and error bars in PDF p. 6, Fig. 2B; they were not read from the figure. Analyzed people counts are not explicitly printed for this contrast, so n_treatment, n_control, and n_total are null; assignment counts and degrees of freedom were not substituted. The omnibus instruction and instruction-by-time tests do not isolate this pair of arms; their F statistics and partial eta-squared effects are not entered as pairwise test or paper_effect values. The procedure separates instruction from the immediate post-test, supporting after_ai; the paper does not explicitly state that ChatGPT access was closed during testing. The p_value is the inclusive bound printed for the set of relevant post hoc comparisons, not an exact pair-specific value. Figure-only annotations were not transcribed under extraction-spec Rule 1. The post hoc analysis uses participant scores; no pairwise SE or CI is printed. Books was also an instructional example, so acquisition may partly reflect recall of ideas encountered during instruction. The paper does not specify how originality ratings of multiple ideas are aggregated within a participant; no sum or mean across ideas is assumed.

During reconciliation, urllib requests to that DOI and the ScienceDirect article URL named in retrieval.json, using User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1, both failed with WinError 10013. Human and Control post-test means and SDs remain null.

The printed AI acquisition flexibility mean and SD conflict with the relative pre/post bar heights in Fig. 2C. The printed text values are retained; the supplement or authors must resolve the discrepancy (PDF pp. 5-6).

Study-wide, arm-specific, and contrast-specific analyzed participant counts are not printed separately from recruitment/randomization counts. All analyzed counts are null; degrees of freedom and sums of randomized arm counts were not used as replacements (PDF p. 3, Section 2.1; PDF pp. 5-6, Section 3.1).

The acquisition originality/flexibility and transfer flexibility comparisons have only shared inclusive p-value bounds in the text. More precise annotations appearing only in Fig. 2 were not transcribed under Rule 1. Transfer originality versus Control has a figure-only pairwise test; its p_value remains null and se_basis is participant. No pairwise test or uncertainty is printed for the remaining fluency comparisons or transfer originality versus Human instruction; these retain se_basis=not_reported.

ChatGPT unavailability during the scored post-test is inferred from the separated instruction and testing phases, rather than explicitly stated. after_ai and outcome_with_ai=false follow that procedure and the reconciled screening form (PDF pp. 4-5, Sections 2.3-2.4; Fig. 1).
Originality aggregation across a participant's ideas is not stated; averaging the raters does not establish averaging or summing the ideas (PDF p. 3, Section 2.2).
The aggregation of umbrellas and can scores into the transfer outcome is not stated (PDF p. 3, Section 2.2; PDF p. 6, Section 3.1).
The model is named ChatGPT-4.0, but the release year and dated model version are not provided, so ai_tool.year is null (PDF p. 4, Section 2.3).

Students is supported by university-advertisement recruitment and the Student labels in Fig. 1A, but enrollment is not explicitly stated. China is inferred from university affiliations and ethics approval, not a direct statement of participant location (PDF pp. 1, 3-4).
notes: Reconciled on 2026-10-10 against the complete saved markdown, including Appendix A and all references, and the cited PDF pages extracted with pymupdf. Figures 1 and 2 were inspected in memory; no image file was created and no figure-only number was transcribed. PDF page indices plus one agree with printed page numbers. All recorded means, SDs and inclusive p-value bounds were checked against the PDF prose; printed precision is preserved in the source quotes. Dispersion following the plus/minus sign is treated as SD consistently with the Fig. 2 caption. Source excerpts are verbatim after normalizing PDF line wrapping and discretionary hyphens. The comparison file lists one substantive field disagreement and no estimates unique to either extractor; that disagreement is resolved in resolutions. B's slugs are retained. All six screening outcomes appear against both comparison arms. Five records have only the printed AI-arm descriptives and the plotted comparator: acquisition fluency versus both arms, transfer fluency versus both arms, and transfer originality versus Human instruction. No pairwise test, difference or effect is asserted for these incomplete records. No additional in-scope outcome or contrast was found. Self-reports, neural outcomes, correlations, baseline tests, omnibus tests, within-arm changes and Human-versus-Control contrasts are listed in not_extracted. Agreed fields were independently checked. PDF p. 1 explicitly reports 95 randomized participants, and PDF p. 3 reports randomized arm counts of 31, 34 and 30. Analyzed counts are not separately printed for the study, arms or creativity contrasts, so all analyzed counts remain null; no degrees of freedom or sums of randomized counts were substituted. PDF p. 3 defines originality as idea originality ratings (novelty; higher_is=more_creative), flexibility as categories within each person's responses (flexibility; higher_is=more_creative), and fluency as valid non-redundant ideas (fluency; higher_is=more_ideas). Ratings are averaged into participant scores, supporting unit=participant and sd_level=participant. PDF pp. 4-5 place instruction before the scored post-test, supporting question=after_ai, outcome_with_ai=false and immediate timing, with explicit post-test AI access left open. The assigned factor is instruction between individuals; repeated pre/post measurements do not justify a randomized-order within-person record, so within_person remains null. AI role is open_chat because participants could request original ideas. Population follows university recruitment and the Student labels in Fig. 1A; country is explicitly marked as an inference from the institutional setting. The paper states no preregistration, primary outcome or shared participant sample. The printed acquisition-flexibility value is retained despite its conflict with Fig. 2C. Missing idea/item aggregation details, model date and supplementary descriptives remain open. Acquisition may reflect recall of books ideas used during instruction; AI-versus-human instruction also differs in communication medium (PDF p. 11, Section 4.4). No standardized effect, difference, SE, interval or participant count was calculated. Only the requested reconciled file was written.

resolutions.decision: participant (A). The AI-versus-Control post-test comparison is explicitly annotated in Fig. 2E, and the scoring method averages raters into participant scores. se_basis describes the paper's own uncertainty, including a reported test whose number is excluded by Rule 1. B incorrectly treated a figure-only test as no reported uncertainty. The figure-only p-value remains null; no SE or CI is inferred.
